question: When the Bank of Canada says it has changed its policy interest rate, which rate is it talking about?
generated_answer:
The Bank of Canada can directly influence a short-term interest rate called the target for the overnight rate. You may have heard it called the policy interest rate. The Bank of Canada uses it to try to meet its inflation target. Economists call the impact the policy rate has on other interest rates the transmission of monetary policy. So, if the Bank changes its policy rate, it affects other interest rates, which then affect people’s spending and borrowing decisions and the economy. The policy interest rate doesn’t control all interest rates, but it does influence them—primarily through short-term risk-free borrowing and lending rates. Transmission of Monetary Policy

How monetary policy works

The whole economy is affected because interest rates influence the value of things like houses, stocks and bonds. If the policy rate increases, other interest rates usually increase, too. That means people who borrow or spend get charged more. It also means people who lend or save are paid more. So, when the policy rate goes up, people are encouraged to save and borrow less. That slows down borrowing and spending in the economy. When the policy rate goes down, the opposite happens. People borrow and spend more. That speeds up borrowing and spending in the economy. The policy interest rate is the target for the overnight rate. This rate is set by the Bank of Canada. The target for the overnight rate sets the interest rate that banks and other financial institutions charge each other for overnight loans. It also influences the loans and mortgages people get from banks. The Bank of Canada changes the policy interest rate to try to meet its inflation target.
